Counterexamples to the x​zxz-Conjecture and the Mathieu Conjecture for S​U​(2)SU(2)

Christopher D. Long Email: galizur@gmail.com
July 21, 2026
Abstract

Let

ℐ⁡(h)=∫01∫𝕋h⁡(x,z)​d​z2​π​i​z​𝑑x(h∈ℂ⁡[x,z,z−1]).\mathcal{I}(h)=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}}h(x,z)\,\frac{dz}{2\pi iz}\,dx\qquad\bigl(h\in\mathbb{C}[x,z,z^{-1}]\bigr).

We give the three-term Laurent polynomial

f⁡(x,z)=(1−z−1)​((1−x)+x​z)f(x,z)=(1-z^{-1})\bigl((1-x)+xz\bigr)

for which

ℐ(fn)=0,ℐ(z−1fn)=(−1)n−1n+1≠0(n≥1).\mathcal{I}(f^{n})=0,\qquad\mathcal{I}(z^{-1}f^{n})=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n+1}\neq 0\qquad(n\geq 1).

Since Sp⁡(f)={−1,0,1}\operatorname{Sp}(f)=\{-1,0,1\}, this disproves the x​zxz-conjecture already with one interval variable and one torus variable, and it also shows that ker⁡ℐ\ker\mathcal{I} is not a Mathieu–Zhao subspace. Padding gives counterexamples to every mixed case of the x​zxz-conjecture. Writing the coordinate functions on S​U​(2)SU(2) as

g=(acbd),g=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\ b&d\end{pmatrix},

the same example lifts, through the integration formula of Müger and Tuset, to the regular functions

F=(1+c)​(a​d+b),G=−c,F=(1+c)(ad+b),\qquad G=-c,

which satisfy

∫S​U​(2)Fn​𝑑g=0,∫S​U​(2)Fn​G​𝑑g=(−1)n−1n+1≠0\int_{SU(2)}F^{n}\,dg=0,\qquad\int_{SU(2)}F^{n}G\,dg=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n+1}\neq 0

for every n≥1n\geq 1. Thus the Mathieu conjecture for S​U​(2)SU(2) is false.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 22E46; Secondary 43A05, 13A50, 14R15.

Keywords. Mathieu conjecture, S​U​(2)SU(2), x​zxz-conjecture, Laurent polynomial, Haar integral, Mathieu–Zhao subspace, Jacobian Conjecture.

1 Introduction

Let KK be a compact connected Lie group with normalized Haar measure d​gdg. Mathieu conjectured that if ff and gg are complex-valued KK-finite functions and

∫Kf​(k)n​𝑑k=0(n≥1),\int_{K}f(k)^{n}\,dk=0\qquad(n\geq 1),

then

∫Kf​(k)n​g​(k)​𝑑k=0\int_{K}f(k)^{n}g(k)\,dk=0

for all sufficiently large nn [6]. Duistermaat and van der Kallen proved the conjecture for compact connected abelian groups [4]. Dings and Koelink studied the first nonabelian case K=S​U​(2)K=SU(2), proving the conjecture for several restricted classes and reducing the general problem to a support conjecture for matrix coefficients [2].

Müger and Tuset subsequently gave an abelian reduction of the S​U​(2)SU(2) problem [7]. For integers k,l≥0k,l\geq 0, an admissible function is a polynomial

h∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xl,z1,z1−1,…,zk,zk−1],h\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{l},z_{1},z_{1}^{-1},\dots,z_{k},z_{k}^{-1}],

written as

h⁡(x,z)=∑m∈ℤkcm​(x)​zm,cm∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xl].h(x,z)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}^{k}}c_{m}(x)z^{m},\qquad c_{m}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{l}].

Its torus spectrum is

Sp⁡(h)={m∈ℤk:cm≠0}.\operatorname{Sp}(h)=\{m\in\mathbb{Z}^{k}:c_{m}\neq 0\}.

The x​zxz-conjecture asserts that

∫[0,1]l∫𝕋kh​(x,z)n​d×​z​𝑑x=0(n≥1)⟹0∉conv⁡Sp⁡(h),\int_{[0,1]^{l}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{k}}h(x,z)^{n}\,d^{\times}z\,dx=0\quad(n\geq 1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0\notin\operatorname{conv}\operatorname{Sp}(h), (1)

where each torus is equipped with normalized Haar measure. The cases l=0l=0 and k=0k=0 were known, while Müger and Tuset recorded that, to the best of their knowledge, every genuinely mixed case was open, including k=l=1k=l=1 [7, Remark 2.4]. They also proved that the case (k,l)=(2,1)(k,l)=(2,1) would imply the Mathieu conjecture for S​U​(2)SU(2) [7, Theorem 2.5].

Mathieu proved that his conjecture for all compact connected Lie groups implies Keller’s Jacobian Conjecture [6, 5]. On July 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge announced an explicit polynomial map in three variables with constant nonzero Jacobian determinant and a fiber containing three distinct points [1]. The determinant and collision identities are direct algebraic checks, so the map disproves the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three and, by adjoining identity coordinates, in every dimension at least three. It follows that Mathieu’s conjecture cannot hold for all compact connected Lie groups. This argument does not determine whether the conjecture holds for S​U​(2)SU(2), nor does it decide the separate x​z​(1,1)xz(1,1) problem. No part of the proofs below depends on the Jacobian counterexample. The examples below settle both questions directly.

Our basic Laurent polynomial is

f⁡(x,z)=(1−z−1)​((1−x)+x​z)=x​z+(1−2​x)−(1−x)​z−1.f(x,z)=(1-z^{-1})\bigl((1-x)+xz\bigr)=xz+(1-2x)-(1-x)z^{-1}. (2)

Its spectrum is the three-point affine circuit

Sp⁡(f)={−1,0,1},\operatorname{Sp}(f)=\{-1,0,1\},

so 0∈conv⁡Sp⁡(f)0\in\operatorname{conv}\operatorname{Sp}(f). Nevertheless, all pure moments vanish. More strongly, the fixed multiplier z−1z^{-1} gives a nonzero mixed moment for every positive exponent.

The mechanism is the elementary beta-binomial identity

(nk)​∫01xk​(1−x)n−k​𝑑x=1n+1.\binom{n}{k}\int_{0}^{1}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx=\frac{1}{n+1}. (3)

It makes every Bernstein stratum contribute with the same normalized weight; the remaining coefficients form an alternating binomial row and cancel exactly.

2 A counterexample to x​z​(1,1)xz(1,1)

Equip 𝕋={z∈ℂ:|z|=1}\mathbb{T}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\} with normalized Haar measure

d×​z=d​z2​π​i​z.d^{\times}z=\frac{dz}{2\pi iz}.

For h∈ℂ⁡[x,z,z−1]h\in\mathbb{C}[x,z,z^{-1}], put

ℐ⁡(h)=∫01∫𝕋h⁡(x,z)​d×​z​𝑑x=∫01CTz⁡h⁡(x,z)​𝑑x.\mathcal{I}(h)=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}}h(x,z)\,d^{\times}z\,dx=\int_{0}^{1}\operatorname{CT}_{z}h(x,z)\,dx. (4)
Theorem 2.1.

Let ff be the polynomial in (2). Then, for every integer n≥1n\geq 1,

ℐ⁡(fn)=0,ℐ⁡(z−1​fn)=(−1)n−1n+1.\mathcal{I}(f^{n})=0,\qquad\mathcal{I}(z^{-1}f^{n})=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n+1}. (5)

Consequently, the x​zxz-conjecture is false for (k,l)=(1,1)(k,l)=(1,1), and ker⁡ℐ\ker\mathcal{I} is not a Mathieu–Zhao subspace of ℂ⁡[x,z,z−1]\mathbb{C}[x,z,z^{-1}].

Proof.

By the binomial theorem,

((1−x)+x​z)n=∑k=0n(nk)​xk​(1−x)n−k​zk.\bigl((1-x)+xz\bigr)^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}z^{k}.

The beta integral gives

∫01xk​(1−x)n−k​𝑑x=k!​(n−k)!(n+1)!=1(n+1)​(nk).\int_{0}^{1}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}=\frac{1}{(n+1)\binom{n}{k}}.

Therefore

∫01((1−x)+x​z)n​𝑑x=1n+1​∑k=0nzk.\int_{0}^{1}\bigl((1-x)+xz\bigr)^{n}\,dx=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^{n}z^{k}. (6)

Using (2), (4), and (6), we obtain

ℐ⁡(fn)\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(f^{n}) =1n+1​CTz​[(1−z−1)n​∑k=0nzk]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n+1}\operatorname{CT}_{z}\left[(1-z^{-1})^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}z^{k}\right]
=1n+1​CTz​[(∑j=0n(−1)j​(nj)​z−j)​(∑k=0nzk)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n+1}\operatorname{CT}_{z}\left[\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j}z^{-j}\right)\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n}z^{k}\right)\right].

A constant term occurs exactly when j=kj=k, so

ℐ⁡(fn)=1n+1​∑j=0n(−1)j​(nj)=(1−1)nn+1=0.\mathcal{I}(f^{n})=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j}=\frac{(1-1)^{n}}{n+1}=0.

For the mixed moment, the constant-term condition in

z−1​(1−z−1)n​∑k=0nzkz^{-1}(1-z^{-1})^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}z^{k}

is −1−j+k=0-1-j+k=0, or k=j+1k=j+1. Hence

ℐ⁡(z−1​fn)\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(z^{-1}f^{n}) =1n+1​∑j=0n−1(−1)j​(nj)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j}
=(−1)n−1n+1,\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n+1},

where the last equality follows by subtracting the final term from ∑j=0n(−1)j​(nj)=0\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j}=0.

Since 0∈conv⁡Sp⁡(f)0\in\operatorname{conv}\operatorname{Sp}(f) while all pure moments vanish, (1) fails for (1,1)(1,1). Finally, fn∈ker⁡ℐf^{n}\in\ker\mathcal{I} for all n≥1n\geq 1, but z−1​fn∉ker⁡ℐz^{-1}f^{n}\notin\ker\mathcal{I} for every n≥1n\geq 1. This is exactly the failure of the Mathieu–Zhao property. ∎

Corollary 2.2.

The x​zxz-conjecture is false for every pair (k,l)(k,l) with k≥1k\geq 1 and l≥1l\geq 1. For every such pair, the kernel of the corresponding product-integration functional is not a Mathieu–Zhao subspace.

Proof.

For larger kk and ll, use the same polynomial f⁡(x1,z1)f(x_{1},z_{1}) and ignore the remaining variables. The product integrals reduce to those in Theorem 2.1, and the multiplier z1−1z_{1}^{-1} gives the same failure of eventual mixed-moment vanishing. ∎

Remark 2.3 (The generating function is constant).

For a Laurent trinomial a​z−1+b+c​zaz^{-1}+b+cz, one has the formal identity

CTz⁡11−t⁡(a​z−1+b+c​z)=1(1−b​t)2−4​a​c​t2,\operatorname{CT}_{z}\frac{1}{1-t(az^{-1}+b+cz)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-bt)^{2}-4act^{2}}},

with the square root having constant term 11. For the polynomial ff in (2),

a=−(1−x),b=1−2​x,c=x,a=-(1-x),\qquad b=1-2x,\qquad c=x,

and the radicand becomes

(1−t⁡(1−2​x))2+4​t2​x​(1−x)=(1−t)2+4​t​x.(1-t(1-2x))^{2}+4t^{2}x(1-x)=(1-t)^{2}+4tx.

Consequently, as a formal power series, or analytically for |t||t| sufficiently small,

1+∑n≥1ℐ⁡(fn)​tn\displaystyle 1+\sum_{n\geq 1}\mathcal{I}(f^{n})t^{n} =∫01d​x(1−t)2+4​t​x\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(1-t)^{2}+4tx}}
=(1+t)2−(1−t)22​t=1.\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{(1+t)^{2}}-\sqrt{(1-t)^{2}}}{2t}=1.

Thus the moment generating function is identically constant; the vanishing is not merely asymptotic or sporadic.

3 A family of circuit counterexamples

The preceding example belongs to a simple family supported on symmetric three-point circuits.

Proposition 3.1.

Let d∈ℤ≥1d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} and let λ,μ∈ℂ×\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}. Define

fd,λ,μ​(x,z)=λ⁡(1−μ​z−d)​((1−x)+x​μ−1​zd).f_{d,\lambda,\mu}(x,z)=\lambda(1-\mu z^{-d})\bigl((1-x)+x\mu^{-1}z^{d}\bigr). (7)

Then

Sp⁡(fd,λ,μ)={−d,0,d},\operatorname{Sp}(f_{d,\lambda,\mu})=\{-d,0,d\},

and, for every n≥1n\geq 1,

ℐ⁡(fd,λ,μn)\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(f_{d,\lambda,\mu}^{n}) =0,\displaystyle=0, (8)
ℐ⁡(z−d​fd,λ,μn)\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(z^{-d}f_{d,\lambda,\mu}^{n}) =(−1)n−1​λn​μ−1n+1.\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}\lambda^{n}\mu^{-1}}{n+1}. (9)
Proof.

Expanding (7) gives

fd,λ,μ=λ​μ−1​x​zd+λ⁡(1−2​x)−λ​μ​(1−x)​z−d,f_{d,\lambda,\mu}=\lambda\mu^{-1}xz^{d}+\lambda(1-2x)-\lambda\mu(1-x)z^{-d},

so its spectrum is {−d,0,d}\{-d,0,d\}. The same beta calculation as in (6) gives

∫01((1−x)+x​μ−1​zd)n​𝑑x=1n+1​∑k=0nμ−k​zd​k.\int_{0}^{1}\bigl((1-x)+x\mu^{-1}z^{d}\bigr)^{n}\,dx=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\mu^{-k}z^{dk}.

Multiplication by

λn​(1−μ​z−d)n=λn​∑j=0n(−1)j​(nj)​μj​z−d​j\lambda^{n}(1-\mu z^{-d})^{n}=\lambda^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j}\mu^{j}z^{-dj}

shows that the pure constant term is

λnn+1​∑j=0n(−1)j​(nj)=0.\frac{\lambda^{n}}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j}=0.

After multiplication by z−dz^{-d}, the constant-term condition is again k=j+1k=j+1, and the powers of μ\mu contribute μj​μ−(j+1)=μ−1\mu^{j}\mu^{-(j+1)}=\mu^{-1}. Thus

ℐ⁡(z−d​fd,λ,μn)=λn​μ−1n+1​∑j=0n−1(−1)j​(nj),\mathcal{I}(z^{-d}f_{d,\lambda,\mu}^{n})=\frac{\lambda^{n}\mu^{-1}}{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{j}\binom{n}{j},

which is (9). ∎

4 The lift to S​U​(2)SU(2)

Write an element of S​U​(2)SU(2) and its coordinate functions as

g=(acbd).g=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\ b&d\end{pmatrix}.

Thus c=−b¯c=-\overline{b}, d=a¯d=\overline{a}, and a​d−b​c=1ad-bc=1 on the group. A regular function on S​U​(2)SU(2) is the restriction of a polynomial in ℂ⁡[a,b,c,d]\mathbb{C}[a,b,c,d]; such functions are S​U​(2)SU(2)-finite. We use normalized Haar measure d​gdg.

Müger and Tuset prove the following integration formula [7, Lemma 2.1]. For completeness, we include a monomial verification. Define

β⁡(z1,z2,x)=((1−x)​z2,x​z1,−z1−1,z2−1).\beta(z_{1},z_{2},x)=\bigl((1-x)z_{2},\;xz_{1},\;-z_{1}^{-1},\;z_{2}^{-1}\bigr). (10)
Lemma 4.1 (The S​U​(2)SU(2) integration formula).

For every P∈ℂ⁡[a,b,c,d]P\in\mathbb{C}[a,b,c,d],

∫S​U​(2)P⁡(a,b,c,d)​𝑑g=∫01∫𝕋2P⁡(β⁡(z1,z2,x))​d​z12​π​i​z1​d​z22​π​i​z2​𝑑x.\int_{SU(2)}P(a,b,c,d)\,dg=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{2}}P\bigl(\beta(z_{1},z_{2},x)\bigr)\frac{dz_{1}}{2\pi iz_{1}}\frac{dz_{2}}{2\pi iz_{2}}\,dx. (11)
Proof.

By linearity it is enough to take

P=ar​bs​ct​du,r,s,t,u∈ℤ≥0.P=a^{r}b^{s}c^{t}d^{u},\qquad r,s,t,u\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

The standard polar description of normalized Haar measure on S​U​(2)SU(2) writes

a=1−x​z2,b=x​z1,c=−x​z1−1,d=1−x​z2−1,a=\sqrt{1-x}\,z_{2},\quad b=\sqrt{x}\,z_{1},\quad c=-\sqrt{x}\,z_{1}^{-1},\quad d=\sqrt{1-x}\,z_{2}^{-1},

where xx is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] and z1,z2z_{1},z_{2} are independently Haar distributed on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. The two torus integrals therefore force r=ur=u and s=ts=t, and the remaining beta integral gives

∫S​U​(2)ar​bs​ct​du​𝑑g=(−1)s​δr,u​δs,t​r!​s!(r+s+1)!.\int_{SU(2)}a^{r}b^{s}c^{t}d^{u}\,dg=(-1)^{s}\delta_{r,u}\delta_{s,t}\frac{r!\,s!}{(r+s+1)!}. (12)

On the right-hand side of (11), the same monomial becomes

(−1)t​(1−x)r​xs​z1s−t​z2r−u.(-1)^{t}(1-x)^{r}x^{s}z_{1}^{s-t}z_{2}^{r-u}.

The torus integrals again force r=ur=u and s=ts=t, after which

∫01(1−x)r​xs​𝑑x=r!​s!(r+s+1)!.\int_{0}^{1}(1-x)^{r}x^{s}\,dx=\frac{r!\,s!}{(r+s+1)!}.

Thus both sides agree with (12), proving the formula. ∎

Theorem 4.2.

Let λ,μ∈ℂ×\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} and define regular functions on S​U​(2)SU(2) by

Fλ,μ=λ⁡(1+μ​c)​(a​d+μ−1​b),G=−c.F_{\lambda,\mu}=\lambda(1+\mu c)(ad+\mu^{-1}b),\qquad G=-c. (13)

Then, for every integer n≥1n\geq 1,

∫S​U​(2)Fλ,μ​(g)n​𝑑g\displaystyle\int_{SU(2)}F_{\lambda,\mu}(g)^{n}\,dg =0,\displaystyle=0, (14)
∫S​U​(2)Fλ,μ​(g)n​G​(g)​𝑑g\displaystyle\int_{SU(2)}F_{\lambda,\mu}(g)^{n}G(g)\,dg =(−1)n−1​λn​μ−1n+1≠0.\displaystyle=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}\lambda^{n}\mu^{-1}}{n+1}\neq 0. (15)

In particular, the Mathieu conjecture for S​U​(2)SU(2) is false.

Proof.

Under the substitution (10),

1+μ​c⟼1−μ​z1−1,a​d+μ−1​b⟼(1−x)+x​μ−1​z1,1+\mu c\longmapsto 1-\mu z_{1}^{-1},\qquad ad+\mu^{-1}b\longmapsto(1-x)+x\mu^{-1}z_{1},

and

G=−c⟼z1−1.G=-c\longmapsto z_{1}^{-1}.

Thus Fλ,μF_{\lambda,\mu} maps precisely to the function f1,λ,μ​(x,z1)f_{1,\lambda,\mu}(x,z_{1}) of Proposition 3.1, while GG maps to z1−1z_{1}^{-1}. These expressions are independent of z2z_{2}, so integration over the second torus contributes the factor 11. Equations (14) and (15) now follow from (11), (8), and (9).

The hypothesis in Mathieu’s conjecture holds for Fλ,μF_{\lambda,\mu}, but its predicted conclusion fails for the fixed regular function GG at every positive exponent. Hence the conjecture is false for S​U​(2)SU(2). ∎

Remark 4.3.

Mathieu’s implication from his compact-group conjecture to the Jacobian Conjecture is one-way. Consequently, Theorem 4.2 does not by itself imply that the two-dimensional Jacobian Conjecture is false.

Taking λ=μ=1\lambda=\mu=1 gives the particularly small pair announced in the abstract:

F=(1+c)​(a​d+b),G=−c.F=(1+c)(ad+b),\qquad G=-c.

The failure of eventual vanishing is maximal in the sense that the mixed moment is nonzero for every n≥1n\geq 1.

5 The cancellation mechanism

The counterexamples arise from an exact interaction between the binomial expansion and the beta integral. For each 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n,

(nk)​∫01xk​(1−x)n−k​𝑑x=1n+1.\binom{n}{k}\int_{0}^{1}x^{k}(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx=\frac{1}{n+1}.

Thus integrating the Bernstein expansion of ((1−x)+x​z)n((1-x)+xz)^{n} removes the binomial coefficient completely and leaves the geometric sum

1n+1​(1+z+⋯+zn).\frac{1}{n+1}(1+z+\cdots+z^{n}).

The factor (1−z−1)n(1-z^{-1})^{n} then contributes the alternating binomial row. The pure moment is the full sum (1−1)n(1-1)^{n}, while multiplication by z−1z^{-1} removes the final term and leaves (−1)n−1(-1)^{n-1}. This explains both the all-moment cancellation and the persistent mixed moments without any limiting argument.

The examples were found during work on the Gaussian Moments Conjecture of Derksen, van den Essen, and Zhao [3]. The contrast is instructive: Gaussian radial moments carry factorial weights, whereas the beta integral in (3) exactly cancels the multinomial coefficient and permits the alternating cancellation above. No result concerning Gaussian moments is needed for the proofs in this paper.
